common_name: Mystical Rainbow Daylily (R.W. Munson, Jr. Award Patterned Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and average, well-drained soil; patterned daylilies show their eye and band markings most clearly when grown in consistent sun rather than part shade.

directions: Hybridized by Patrick Stamile, 'Mystical Rainbow' received the American Hemerocallis Society's R. W. Munson, Jr. Award in 2003, an honor established in 2001 for the most outstanding daylily showing a pattern beyond a simple eye, band, or watermark. The specific color layout of this particular cultivar is not detailed in the sources consulted for this entry, a gap common to earlier winners of the award whose photographs circulated mainly through regional show records rather than wide retail listings. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep the patterned bloom reading cleanly against the foliage.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society (AHS) — R. W. Munson, Jr. Award records

common_name: Web of Intrigue Daylily (R.W. Munson, Jr. Award Patterned Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, giving the clump room to bulk up so its patterned eye zone shows on multiple scapes at once.

directions: Registered by Stamile, 'Web of Intrigue' won the American Hemerocallis Society's R. W. Munson, Jr. Award in 2007, recognizing it as the year's most outstanding patterned cultivar under the award's broad definition covering feathered, stippled, streaked, or otherwise variegated bloom designs. Sources consulted for this entry do not preserve a detailed account of the cultivar's own color combination, so growers should treat it as an award-documented patterned selection rather than a confirmed specific hue. Give it full sun and divide every three to four years as clumps thicken, standard care for tetraploid and diploid patterned daylilies alike.

common_name: Etched Eyes Daylily (R.W. Munson, Jr. Award Patterned Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; established clumps of this patterned cultivar reward light annual feeding with heavier bud count.

directions: Hybridized by Matthew Kaskel, 'Etched Eyes' took the American Hemerocallis Society's R. W. Munson, Jr. Award in 2002, among the earliest winners of an honor created the previous year specifically to recognize patterned daylilies as a distinct breeding category. As with many early-2000s winners of this award, no further written description of its particular eye or pattern coloring was found in the sources consulted. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring and keep the planting in full sun to maintain strong bloom production.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society (AHS) — R. W. Munson, Jr. Award records

common_name: Texas Kaleidoscope Daylily (R.W. Munson, Jr. Award Patterned Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; give the clump a few seasons to mature before expecting the full patterned display the award recognized.

directions: Bred by Jack B. Carpenter, 'Texas Kaleidoscope' earned the American Hemerocallis Society's R. W. Munson, Jr. Award in 2010 for the year's outstanding patterned-bloom cultivar, a category named for hybridizer R.W. Munson Jr.'s pioneering work with watermark patterning. The exact pattern layout on this particular introduction is not recorded in the sources consulted here. Divide every three to four years once clumps become congested, and grow in full sun for the clearest pattern expression.

common_name: Broadway Attraction Daylily (Florida Sunshine Cup Miniature Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun; miniature-flowered daylilies like this one suit front-of-border placement where their smaller blooms and shorter scapes are not overshadowed by larger-flowered neighbors.

directions: Hybridized by Grace Stamile, 'Broadway Attraction' won the American Hemerocallis Society's Florida Sunshine Cup in 2007, a convention-attendee-voted award for the most outstanding small- or miniature-flowered clump touring gardens that year. No specific bloom-color description for this introduction survives in the sources consulted here, though its award confirms a small flower size and strong garden performance as a clump. Divide every three to four years in spring and keep plantings in full sun to sustain the heavy bud count typical of award-winning miniatures.

common_name: Witches Wink Daylily (Florida Sunshine Cup Miniature Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun, siting this miniature along a path or border edge where its compact scapes are easy to view up close.

directions: Registered by E.H. Salter, 'Witches Wink' received the American Hemerocallis Society's Florida Sunshine Cup in 2008, chosen by vote of AHS National Convention tour-garden attendees as that year's best small- or miniature-flowered clump. The sources consulted for this entry do not preserve a detailed color description, only the award record itself. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring and grow in full sun to keep bud count high on this compact-flowered selection.

common_name: Debary Canary Daylily (Ned Roberts Spider/Unusual Form Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, allowing room at the back of the border since spider and unusual-form daylilies often carry unusually tall or long-petaled scapes.

directions: Hybridized by Patrick Stamile, 'Debary Canary' won the American Hemerocallis Society's Ned Roberts Spider/Unusual Form Award in 2008, a Region 9-administered honor voted on by AHS National Convention tour-garden attendees for the best spider or unusual-form clump of the year. Its own petal proportions and coloring are not spelled out in the sources consulted for this entry, which record only the award and hybridizer. Give it full sun and stake tall scapes in windy sites, then divide congested clumps every three to four years to sustain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Green Inferno Daylily (Ned Roberts Spider/Unusual Form Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun; give this unusual-form selection extra room since the award category typically favors cultivars with dramatic, elongated petal shapes.

directions: Hybridized by James Gossard, a breeder known for narrow-petaled patterned spider forms, 'Green Inferno' took the American Hemerocallis Society's Ned Roberts Spider/Unusual Form Award in 2015 as voted by AHS National Convention tour-garden attendees. The name suggests a strongly chartreuse-to-green coloring, but no confirmed written color record for this specific introduction was found in the sources consulted. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring and grow in full sun to keep the distinctive form reading clearly on the scape.
